entry.title: NTK: A First Principles Derivation
entry.content:
Neural Tangent Kernel or NTK by (Jacot et al., 2018) is arguably one of the first very deep theoretical insights about neural networks in the mean-field (infinitely wide) regime. While nowadays its importance has been surpassed by the feature learning (muP) regime, it is nevertheless one of the classical papers that are worth fully understanding for any researcher in the deep learning community with theoretical inclinations. However, I have heard from virtually everyone I have talked to that the paper is very hard, if not impossible, to read, which is of course a big pity. To be very honest, my initial attempt at reading the paper was also met with a lot of hiccups. So at some point, I decided to “reinvent the wheel” by proving essentially all the key results of the paper, without reading the paper. This note is the result of my efforts. While there might be some mistakes here and there (which I would be thankful if you report them to me!), I believe the method shown here replicates all the technical results of the NTK paper. The key aspect of these derivations is that they are completely from scratch. I do not assume anything beyond a few basic mathematical facts, namely the law of large numbers, CLT, and a few tricks about the expectation of Gaussians (Stein’s lemma).

Towards the end of the document, there is an exposition of my effort to verify or correct an assumption that I had made in my first attempt about the independence of backwards from forwards. These effects manifest themselves in our algebraic framework as “non-diagonal” terms in the backward kernel (meaning interactions between backwards that correspond to different units). These are exactly the terms that we will ignore if we assume independence of forward and backward, which allows us to use the expectation of product rule and get a very simple straightforward solution. The issue that I originally thought existed was that the number of these interactions could be of the same order as they are decaying, meaning that they could contribute significantly to the backward kernel. The calculations, which admittedly went a lot longer than I had hoped for, showed the opposite. Meaning, they proved these corrections are in fact an order of magnitude smaller than the main terms. I still kept these notes for anyone interested. But feel free to ignore them if not.

Setup: The Infinite-Width (Mean-Field) Regime

We begin by defining the precise mathematical setting for our analysis.

We consider a fully-connected neural network with an input layer, \(L-1\) hidden layers with widths \(d_1,\dots, d_{L-1}\), and a scalar output layer \(d_L=1\), for a total of \(L\) layers of activations.

  • Layer 0 (Input): $h^0(x) = x \in \mathbb{R}^{d_0}$
  • Hidden Layers ($1 \leq l < L$):

\begin{align} &z^l(x) = W^{l-1} h^{l-1}(x) + b^{l-1} && \text{(Pre-activation)} \cr &h^{l-1}(x) = \phi(z^{l-1}(x)) && \text{(Activation)} \cr &z^L(x) = W^{L-1} h^{L-1}(x) + b^{L-1} && \text{(output, scalar)} \end{align}

The weights and biases are initialized as i.i.d. zero-mean Gaussian variables with fan-in variance scaling: \(\begin{align} W^{l}_{ij} &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_w^2 / d_{l}) \\ b^{l}_i &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_b^2) \end{align}\)

Loss: For simplicity, as specified in the analysis, we define the loss to be the network output itself, evaluated at an input $x’$: \(\mathcal{L} = z^L(x')\). This captures the essential structure of the gradients without loss of generality.

Kernel in the Mean-Field Regime

The kernel at layer \(l\) between \(x\) and \(x'\) is defined as the average inner product of their layer \(l\) pre-activations: \begin{align} \Sigma^l(x,x’) := \frac{1}{d_l} \langle z^l(x), z^l(x’) \rangle \end{align}

It is straightforward to show the following forward recursion for the kernel in the mean-field regime:

\begin{align} \Sigma^0(x,x’) &:= \sigma_w^2 \frac{1}{d_0} x^\top x’ + \sigma_b^2\cr \Sigma^{l+1}(x,x’) &:= \sigma_w^2 \mathbb{E}\left[\phi(z)\phi(z’)\right] + \sigma_b^2 && \text{where } (z,z’)\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma^l(x,x’)) \end{align}

Similar to the NTK paper, we can use a more specialized notation to denote the derivatives kernel at a specified layer: \begin{align} \dot \Sigma^l(x,x’) &:= \sigma_w^2 \mathbb{E} [\phi’(z)\phi’(z’)] && \text{where } (z,z’)\sim \mathcal{N}\left(0, \Sigma^{l-1}(x,x’)\right) \end{align}

We are interested in how the network representations change under the influence of the gradient of the loss $\mathcal{L} = z^L(x’)$. Specifically, we analyze the change in the pre-activation $z^l(x)$ caused by updating the weights of layer $k-1$, which we denote $\Theta_{k,l}$.

The change in the kernel $\Sigma^l$ is a sum of terms. A representative term, which we denote $\dot{\Theta}_{k,l}$, captures the influence of the gradient with respect to weights $W^{k-1}$ on the correlation between $z^l(x)$ and the loss $z^L(x’)$:

\[\dot{\Theta}_{k,l} := \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i=1}^{d_l}\left\langle \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial W^{k-1}}, \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial W^{k-1}} \right\rangle _{W^{k-1}}\]

where $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle_{W^{k-1}}$ denotes the Frobenius inner product over all elements of the weight matrix $W^{k-1}$. Using the outer product rule for gradients ($\nabla_W (Wa) = a^\top I$), this decomposes into:

\[\dot{\Theta}_{k,l} = \langle h^{k-1}(x), h^{k-1}(x') \rangle \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i=1}^{d_l} \left\langle \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial z^k}, \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial z^k} \right\rangle_{z^k}\]

The first term, $\langle h^{k-1}(x), h^{k-1}(x’) \rangle$, is the inner product of activations from the forward pass. At large width $d$, this term is well-behaved and of order $O(d)$. Our focus is therefore on the second term, which involves the Jacobians of the backward passes.

To formalize the analysis of its mean and variance, we define two key quantities:

Definition (Kernel Shift). The first, second, and variance of the kernel shift are defined as:

\[\begin{align} M_{k,l} &:= \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i=1}^{d_l} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{d_k} \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial z^k_j} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial z^k_j} \right] &&\text{(first moment)}\\ Q_{k,l} &= \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i=1}^{d_l} \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{j=1}^{d_k} \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial z^k_j} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial z^k_j}\right)^2\right] && \text{(second moment)}\\ V_{k,l} &:= Q_{k,l} - M_{k,l}^2 && \text{(variance)} \end{align}\]

Intuitively, we can understand these two terms as the average shift in representation of layer $l$, in expectation ($M$), and variance ($V$).

Remark. The averaging over indices $i$ represents computing the sample mean and sample variance over the features. However, due to symmetry in these indices, all expected terms in $i$ will result in equal values, meaning that we can simply replace this by a formula that fixes one $i$ and removes summation and averaging. The reason for keeping the averaging in place will be revealed later. In short, this has to do with the recursive step of the proof, and the average formulation allows us to arrive at a clean inductive step.

We will derive recursions for $M$ and $V$ to determine their scaling with width.

Recursion for the Mean Influence

A very important and clear fact is the Jacobian of two successive layers:

\[\partial z^{l+1}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{d_l} W^l_{ij} \phi(z^l_j) + b_i \implies \frac{\partial z^{l+1}_i}{\partial z^l_j} = W^l_{ij}\phi'(z^l_j)\]

Substituting this into the definition of $M_{k,l}$, we can expand the formula from $k$ to the next layer $k+1$:

\[\begin{align} M_{k,l} &:= \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i=1}^{d_l} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{d_k} \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial z^k_j} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial z^k_j} \right]\\ &= \frac{1}{d_l}\sum_{i,j} \mathbb{E}\left[ \left( \sum_{s} \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial z^{k+1}_s} \frac{\partial z^{k+1}_s(x)}{\partial z^k_j} \right) \left( \sum_{r} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial z^{k+1}_r(x')} \frac{\partial z^{k+1}_r(x')}{\partial z^{k}_j} \right) \right] \\ &= \frac{1}{d_l}\sum_{i,j} \mathbb{E}\left[ \left( \sum_{s} \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial z^{k+1}_s} W^k_{sj} \phi'(z^k_j(x)) \right) \left( \sum_{r} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial z^{k+1}_r} W^k_{rj} \phi'(z^k_j(x')) \right) \right] \\ &= \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i,j,s,r} \mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial z^{k+1}_s} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial z^{k+1}_r} \phi'(z^k_j(x))\phi'(z^k_j(x')) W^k_{sj} W^k_{rj} \right] \end{align}\]

The independence of weight elements: This is the first subtle argument in our proof method, which argues that we can move the expectation with respect to weights forward to act only on the terms involving layer $k$ weights. This is justified because in the mean-field limit ($d \to \infty$), succeeding layers are asymptotically independent of any single weight element $W^k_{sj}$. This might present itself as contradictory, given the obvious dependence of layer $z^{k+1}$ and succeeding layers on weight matrix $W^k$. The nuance is in the distinction between the entire matrix vs. the individual elements of the matrix. Because of the way that we initialize the weights from $\mathcal{N}(0,1/d)$, the influence of every individual element of $W^k$ on the succeeding layer $z^{k+1}$ decays with $d$, which means that the $W^{k}_{ij}$ terms are effectively independent of all other terms in the formula above. This allows us to use the product rule for expectation of independent random variables:

\[M_{k,l} = \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i,j,s,r} \mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial z^{k+1}_s} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial z^{k+1}_r} \phi'(z^k_j(x))\phi'(z^k_j(x')) \right] \mathbb{E}[W^k_{sj} W^k_{rj}]\]

The pairing of weights. Since weight elements are assumed to be drawn i.i.d. and zero-mean, the expectation $\mathbb{E}[W^k_{sj} W^k_{rj}]$ is non-zero only if the weights are paired with each other to form random variables of even power. This can happen if and only if we have $r=s$, which requires their indices to match: \(\mathbb{E}[W^k_{sj} W^k_{rj}] = \delta_{sr} \frac{\sigma_w^2}{d_k}\)

Since all other terms vanish, we can enforce this pairing by setting $r = s$ in our summation: \(\frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i,j,s} \mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial z^{k+1}_s} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial z^{k+1}_s} \phi'(z^k_j(x))\phi'(z^k_j(x')) \right] \left(\frac{\sigma_w^2}{d_k}\right)\)

Note that here the pairing argument was trivial because we only had two weight elements to begin with.

CLT: We can move the summation over $j$ forward and rearrange the terms: \(\frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i,s} \mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial z^{k+1}_s} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial z^{k+1}_s} \left(\frac{\sigma_w^2}{d_k}\sum_{j=1}^{d_k} \phi'(z^k_j(x))\phi'(z^k_j(x')) \right)\right]\)

Given that the averaging involving $j$ in the second term involves terms that are i.i.d, this sample average converges to its expectation in the limit of $d_l\to\infty$: \(M_{k,l} = \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i,s} \mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial z^{k+1}_s} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial z^{k+1}_s}\right]\left[\sigma_w^2 \mathbb{E} \left[\phi'(z)\phi'(z')\right]\right]\) where $(z,z’)\sim \mathcal{N}\left(0, \Sigma^{k-1}(x,x’)\right)$.

Using our notation for derivatives kernel and if we rearrange the constants around we arrive at: \(M_{k,l} = \dot \Sigma^{k}(x,x') \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i,s} \mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial z^{k+1}_s} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial z^{k+1}_s} \right]\)

If we carefully inspect the formula above, we can recognize the recursive formula inside the second term which finishes our first recursive step: \(M_{k,l} = \dot \Sigma^{k}(x,x') M_{k+1,l}\)

To complete the proof we have to also prove some basis for our recursion. It is clear from our setup and proof that this is restricted to cases where $k+1\le l$. Therefore, a natural basis for this particular inductive argument is $k=l$. Thus, we can unroll this recursion from $k$ to $l$: \(M_{k,l} = M_{l,l} \prod_{i=k}^{l-1}\dot \Sigma^{i}(x,x')\)

Induction Basis for Mean Influence

Recall the definition of $M$: \(M_{k,l} := \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i=1}^{d_l} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{d_l}\frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial z^k_j} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial z^k_j} \right]\)

Now we can create the basis by setting $k=l$. It is clear from the partial derivatives that only the $i=j$ term survives: \(M_{l,l} = \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i=1}^{d_l} \mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial z^l_i} \right]\)

We can now divide it into two cases depending on $l=L$ or not:

  1. $l=L$ case: This is a trivial case, because now we simply have one index $i=1$ and $d_L = 1$, and the partial derivative is simply $1$. Therefore we have: \(M_{L,L} = 1\)

  2. $l<L$ case: We can use the same unrolling trick used above to now induct over $l$ upwards. From now on, because we’re only working with $x’$, we will drop it from our terms: \(\begin{align} M_{l,l} &= \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i=1}^{d_l} \mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{\partial z^L}{\partial z^l_i} \right]\\ &=\frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i,j} \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial z^L}{\partial z^{l+1}_j} \frac{\partial z^{l+1}_j}{\partial z^l_i}\right] \\ &=\frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i,j} \mathbb{E} \left[\frac{\partial z^L}{\partial z^{l+1}_j} W_{ji}^l\phi'(z^l_i)\right] \end{align}\)

Here, we can apply the same principles as before to isolate the weight terms, which in this case will simply imply that this term will vanish: \(M_{l,l} = 0 \quad \forall l<L\)

Combining the two base cases we now have: \(M_{k,l} = \begin{cases} 0 & l < L\\ \prod_{i=k}^{L-1} \dot\Sigma^i(x,x') & l=L \end{cases}\)

To finalize the first moment kernel evolution, we have to compute the product with the forward of layer $k-1$ and apply our learning rate. Choosing the layer-specific learning rate $\eta$ per layer. Here, we make one of the most important and consequential decisions of our setup with respect to learning rate which will dictate our learning rate regime from here onward. We will assume that while we are tending all our middle layers to infinity, we inversely scale learning rate per layer as $\eta_l \propto \eta_0 /d_l$, where $\eta_0$ is some master learning rate that can be a width-invariant constant.

Thus, the combined effect of learning rate, forward products, and backward product can be written as $\eta_0 /d_{k-1} \langle h^{k-1}(x), h^{k-1}(x’)\rangle$ multiplied by the backward result $M_{k,l}$. Recall that our forward recursion gives us $\Sigma^{k-1}(x,x’)$ implying that $\frac{1}{d_{k-1}} \langle h^{k-1}(x), h^{k-1}(x’)\rangle \to \Sigma^{k-1}(x,x’)$ as $d_{k-1}$ grows. Thus we can replace the average with expectation again to obtain: \(\mathbb{E} [\dot\Theta_{k,l}] = \begin{cases} 0 & l < L\\ \eta_0 \Sigma^{k-1}(x,x')\prod_{i=k}^{L-1} \dot\Sigma^i(x,x') & l=L \end{cases}\)

Now, we can observe the following highly important remark:

Remark. We have thus concluded that only the final layer has a non-vanishing first moment. The second point is that, while the first moment for last layer kernel shift is a product of several terms, it is crucially width-independent. This means if we scale the width and learning rates accordingly, the result will be a kernel shift that is constant.

The product terms are tightly related to an important concept in signal propagation.

Remark. Observe that if we set $x=x’$, the derivative kernel $\dot\Sigma^l(x,x’)$ will take the more familiar term of $\mathbb{E} [\phi’(z)^2]$ where $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,q_l)$, where $q_l$ denotes the variance of layer $l$ pre-activations, itself obeying $q_{l+1} = \mathbb{E} [\phi(\sqrt{q_l}z)^2]$. If we assume that the variance sequence converges in depth to some fixed point $q_l \to q^*$, as depth grows, this value is referred to as $\chi_1$ in the deep signal propagation and edge of chaos literature. This implies that the mean shift in the last layer’s kernel evolution is always bounded by $(\chi_1)^{L-l}$. Otherwise, if we configure a neural network to operate at the edge of chaos $\chi_1 = 1$, the kernel first moment of shift is always bounded by $1$.

The Variance of Kernel Shifts

To complete this picture, we also need to understand the fluctuations around the mean kernel shifts. To assess the variance, we will evaluate the second moments of kernel shifts very carefully, and then use the variance formula (second moment minus first moment squared) to evaluate the variance.

Our strategy to analyze the second moment is highly similar to the one for first moment. However, it will be more involved due to the presence of a double summation as a result of squaring in the second moment.

\[\begin{align} Q_{k,l} &= \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i=1}^{d_l} \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{j=1}^{d_k} \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial z^k_j} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial z^k_j}\right)^2\right] \\ &= \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i=1}^{d_l} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{j,r,s} \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial z^{k+1}_r} \frac{\partial z^{k+1}_r(x)}{\partial z^k_j} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial z^{k+1}_s} \frac{\partial z^{k+1}_s(x')}{\partial z^k_j} \right] \\ &= \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i=1}^{d_l} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{j,r,s} \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial z^{k+1}_r} W_{rj}^k\phi'(z^k_j(x)) \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial z^{k+1}_s} W_{sj}^k\phi'(z^k_j(x')) \right] \end{align}\]

Now, if we are to follow our strategy from before we have to again expand our indices, introducing $j’,r’,s’$, to account for the power of two. To follow our main strategy, we will isolate all the terms involving $z^k$ or $W^k$ on the right-most side, resulting in the summation:

\[\frac{1}{d_l}\mathbb{E} \sum \left(\frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial z^{k+1}_r} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial z^{k+1}_s} \frac{\partial z^l_{i}(x)}{\partial z^{k+1}_{r'}} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial z^{k+1}_{s'}} \right)\cdot \left( \phi'(z^k_j(x)) \phi'(z^k_j(x')) \phi'(z^k_{j'}(x)) \phi'(z^k_{j'}(x')) \right) \left(W_{rj}^k W_{sj}^k W_{r'j'}^k W_{s'j'}^k \right)\]

where the summation is over all indices $i,j,r,s,j’,r’,s’$.

At this point, we can use the fact of independence of weight elements from the rest to isolate the weight product terms. Here, we use Wick’s theorem to convert our fourth-order expectation to a simpler form based on the formula $\mathbb{E} [X_1 X_2 X_3 X_4] = \mathbb{E} [X_1 X_2] \mathbb{E} [X_3 X_4] + \mathbb{E} [X_1 X_3] \mathbb{E} [X_2 X_4] + \mathbb{E} [X_1 X_4] \mathbb{E} [X_2 X_3]$. We have:

\[\begin{align} &\mathbb{E} \left(W_{rj}^k W_{sj}^k W_{r'j'}^k W_{s'j'}^k \right) = \\ &\qquad \mathbb{E} [W_{rj}^k W_{sj}^k] \mathbb{E} [W_{r'j'}^k W_{s'j'}^k] + \mathbb{E} [W_{rj}^k W_{r'j'}^k ] \mathbb{E} [ W_{sj}^k W_{s'j'}^k ] + \mathbb{E} [W_{rj}^k W_{s'j'}^k] \mathbb{E} [W_{sj}^k W_{r'j'}^k ] \end{align}\]

Now, after summation is over all indices $j,j’\le d_k$, and $r,r’,s,s’\le d_{k+1}$. Now, in order to count the pairings as we sum over all these indices, we need to enforce each pair of weights to have exactly equal indices, and then count how many such pairings exist.

  1. First term: $r=s, r’=s’$. Thus we have $d_k^2 d_{k+1}^2$ remaining terms.
  2. Second term: $r=r’, j=j’, s=s’$. Thus we have $d_k d_{k+1}^2$ remaining terms.
  3. Third term: $r=s’, j=j’, s=r’$: this is symmetric to the second term and is also $d_k d_{k+1}^2$ counts.

This calculation reveals that the first configuration will be the leading order, with the second and third term $O(1/d_k)$ relative to the first term.

After accounting for the weight variances and applying coefficient $\sigma_w^4/d_k^2$, all terms except for the downstream partial derivatives can be written as:

\[\begin{align} &\text{sum over } z^k\text{'s and } W^k\text{'s}\\ &\qquad =\sum_{j,j'} (\sigma_w^4/d_k^2) \left( \phi'(z^k_j(x)) \phi'(z^k_j(x')) \phi'(z^k_{j'}(x)) \phi'(z^k_{j'}(x')) \right) \\ &\qquad= \left(\frac{\sigma_w^2}{d_k}\sum_{j=1}^{d_k}\phi'(z^k_j(x)) \phi'(z^k_j(x'))\right)^2\\ &\qquad= (\dot\Sigma^k(x,x'))^2 \end{align}\]

where in the last step we again used the CLT and used the definition of derivative kernel. Note that at this point, we can assume that the second leading order $O(1/d_k)$ is smaller than this term due to the terms that we ignored.

We can now plug this result into our main second moment formula: \(\begin{align} Q_{k,l} &= \dot\Sigma^k(x,x')^2\frac{1}{d_l}\mathbb{E} \sum_{i,r,r'} \left( \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial z^{k+1}_r} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial z^{k+1}_r} \frac{\partial z^l_{i}(x)}{\partial z^{k+1}_{r'}} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial z^{k+1}_{r'}} \right)\\ &= \dot\Sigma^k(x,x')^2\frac{1}{d_l}\mathbb{E} \sum_{i=1}^{d_l} \left( \left[\sum_{r=1}^{d_{k+1}} \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial z^{k+1}_r} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial z^{k+1}_{r}} \right]^2\right)\\ &=\dot\Sigma^k(x,x')^2 Q_{k+1,l} \end{align}\)

Where in the last step we again have identified our recursive formula in the step above it. We can now roll this induction step forward until arriving at $Q_{l,l}$: \(Q_{k,l} = Q_{l,l}\prod_{i=k}^{l-1}(\dot\Sigma^i(x,x'))^2\)

It is important to note that this is the leading order, and the approximation factor will be $O(1/d_k)$ relative to this result.

To arrive at a concrete result, we again have to find a basis. For that, we have to consider the $Q_{l,l}$ case separately.

\[\begin{align} Q_{l,l} &= \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i=1}^{d_l} \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{j=1}^{d_l} \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial z^l_j} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial z^l_j}\right)^2\right] \\ &= \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i=1}^{d_l} \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial z^l_i}\right)^2\right] \end{align}\]

First, note that if $l=L$ then we have only one term $d_L=1$ and that term is identity, implying $Q_{L,L} = 1$. We can again expand this by chain rule and roll it forward. We can now ignore the argument $x’$ as there is no counterpart:

\[\begin{align} Q_{l,l} &= \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i=1}^{d_l} \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_j \frac{\partial z^L}{\partial z^{l+1}_j}\frac{\partial z^{l+1}_j}{\partial z^l_i}\right)^2\right] \\ &= \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i=1}^{d_l} \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_j \frac{\partial z^L}{\partial z^{l+1}_j}W_{ji}^l\phi'(z_i^l)\right)^2\right] \\ &= \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i,j,j'} \mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{\partial z^L}{\partial z^{l+1}_j}W_{ji}^l\phi'(z_i^l)\frac{\partial z^L}{\partial z^{l+1}_{j'}}W_{j'i}^l\phi'(z_i^l)\right] \\ &= \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i,j,j'} \mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{\partial z^L}{\partial z^{l+1}_j}\frac{\partial z^L}{\partial z^{l+1}_{j'}} \phi'(z_i^l)\phi'(z_i^l) \right]\cdot \mathbb{E} \left[W_{ji}^lW_{j'i}^l\right] \\ &= \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i,j} \mathbb{E}\left[ \left(\frac{\partial z^L}{\partial z^{l+1}_j}\right)^2 (\phi'(z_i^l))^2\right] \cdot \mathbb{E}[(W_{ji}^l)^2] \\ &= \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{i,j} \mathbb{E}\left[ \left(\frac{\partial z^L}{\partial z^{l+1}_j}\right)^2 (\phi'(z_i^l))^2\right] \frac{\sigma_w^2}{d_l} \\ &= \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{j} \mathbb{E}\left[ \left(\frac{\partial z^L}{\partial z^{l+1}_j}\right)^2 \right] \left(\frac{\sigma_w^2}{d_l}\sum_i (\phi'(z_i^l))^2\right) \end{align}\]

Again, in our last line we can recognize the CLT argument to write: \(Q_{l,l} = \frac{1}{d_l} \sum_{j} \mathbb{E}\left[ \left(\frac{\partial z^L}{\partial z^{l+1}_j}\right)^2 \right] \left(\sigma_w^2 \mathbb{E} [(\phi'(z))^2]\right) \quad \text{where } z\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma^l(x'))\)

We can reorder the terms and recognize the recursive formula: \(Q_{l,l} =Q_{l+1,l+1} \dot\Sigma^l(x') \frac{d_{l+1}}{d_l}\)

And finally, we can roll the induction forward first to get from $Q_{k,l}$ to $Q_{l,l}$ using the first induction, and then to $Q_{L,L} = 1$ using the second induction, and use the hypothesis to conclude: \(\begin{align} Q_{l,l} &= Q_{L,L}\prod_{i=l}^{L-1} \frac{d_{i+1}}{d_i}\prod_{i=l}^{L-1}\dot\Sigma^i(x',x') \\ &= 1\cdot \frac{d_L}{d_l}\prod_{i=l}^{L-1}\dot\Sigma^i(x',x')\\ &= \frac{1}{d_l}\prod_{i=l}^{L-1}\dot\Sigma^i(x',x') \end{align}\)

Thus, combining the two cases we have: \(Q_{k,l} = \frac{1}{d_l}\left(\prod_{i=k}^{l-1}(\dot\Sigma^i(x,x'))^2\right) \cdot \left(\prod_{i=l}^{L-1}\dot\Sigma^i(x',x')\right)\)

Now, in order to account for the second moment variations due to applying gradient update, we need to account for the learning rate of $W^k$, as well as the forward product $d_{k-1}\Sigma^{k-1}(x,x’)$, both of which will be squared. Recall that we applied a learning rate of $\eta_0/d_{k-1}$ to this layer. Thus the cumulative effect will be that $\eta_0/d_{k-1} \langle h^{k-1}(x),h^{k-1}(x’)\rangle$ converges to its expectation $\eta_0 \Sigma^{k-1}(x,x’)$. Because we’re analyzing the second moment, both the effect of learning rate and the inner product of forwards will be squared. Thus we have the second moment:

\[\mathbb{E} [(\dot\Theta_{k,l})^2] = \frac{1}{d_l} (\eta_0\Sigma^{k-1}(x,x'))^2\left(\prod_{i=k}^{l-1}(\dot\Sigma^i(x,x'))^2\right) \cdot \left(\prod_{i=l}^{L-1}\dot\Sigma^i(x',x')\right)\]

which is accurate up to $O(\sum_{l=1}^L 1/d_l)$ approximation factor. This is the result of our inductive step where in each step we introduce a $(1+O(L/d_k))$ approximation factor, which we can upper bound by using the worst (narrowest layer).

Now, recall the result for first moments: \(\mathbb{E} [\dot\Theta_{k,l}] = \begin{cases} 0 & l < L\\ \eta_0 \Sigma^{k-1}(x,x')\prod_{i=k}^{L-1} \dot\Sigma^i(x,x') & l=L \end{cases}\)

In order to obtain variance we can now use the second moment minus first moment squared formula. Observe that the leading order of the terms for second moment layer $L$ is equal to the square of the first moment. This means, the entire variance must be captured by the approximation error. We thus have:

\[\text{Var} [\dot\Theta_{k,l}] = \begin{cases} \frac{\eta_0^2}{d_l} (\Sigma^{k-1}(x,x'))^2\left(\prod_{i=k}^{l-1}(\dot\Sigma^i(x,x'))^2\right) \cdot \left(\prod_{i=l}^{L-1}\dot\Sigma^i(x',x')\right) & l < L\\ \sum_{k}^{l} O(1/d_k)\eta_0^2 (\Sigma^{k-1}(x,x'))^2\left(\prod_{i=k}^{l-1}(\dot\Sigma^i(x,x'))^2\right) & l=L \end{cases}\]

It is clear that if we now tend all hidden layers to infinity $d_1,\dots, d_{L-1} \to \infty$, both variances will vanish. This means, both mean values indicate a deterministic scenario that there is zero variance.

Putting It All Together

So far we have only considered isolated influence terms. In order to analyze the kernel evolution, we need to sum up all different terms. In the second moment analysis, this means computing cross terms of type $\mathbb{E} [\dot \Theta_{k,l}\dot \Theta_{k’,l}]$ where $k\neq k’$. Here, we can rely on the body of work laid out here to argue that these cross terms will vanish, because assuming without loss of generality $k < k’$, the weight terms $W^k$ cannot be paired with any other term, and hence, the entire cross term will vanish. Therefore, both mean and variance of the kernel shift at $l$ will be simply equal to the sum of all influence terms from $k=1$ up until $k=L$. As we know by now, the variances were already vanishing, and the mean of middle-layers was also vanishing. Thus, here we will only focus on the last layer kernel shift first moment, which is the sum of all terms leading up to it:

\[\dot\Theta^L = \sum_{k=1}^L \dot \Theta_{k,L} = \sum_{k=1}^L \eta_0 \Sigma^{k-1}(x,x')\prod_{i=k}^{L-1}\dot\Sigma^i(x,x')\]

Note that here we have dropped the expectation, because by now we know that these are deterministic quantities with zero variance.

From this formula, it is not hard to notice the famous recursion of NTK: \(\dot\Theta^L = \eta_0\Sigma^{L-1}(x,x')+\dot\Theta^{L-1}\dot\Sigma^{L-1}(x,x')\)

This finishes our NTK derivations and establishes all the key facts in that paper.

A More Nuanced First Moment Calculation

After reviewing my proof above, which replicates the NTK result, I’ve realized a flaw in the argument. More concretely, I tried to make a subtle assumption of independence more rigorous. But as I made it more rigorous, it became clear that there is no easy way of bounding it without rigorously working out all the details. Somewhat annoyingly, after a very long and laborious sequence of calculations, this resulted in the same qualitative result, as in, it did not alter the main result of NTK recursion.

Heart of the problem: At the heart of this discrepancy is the following observation: Suppose that elements of $W$ are drawn i.i.d. from $\mathcal{N}(0,1/d)$, and construct $h=\phi(z(W x))$ where $x$ is some input vector that represents post-activations of the previous layer. In my previous analysis, whenever terms like $\phi’(z_s)\phi’(z_r)W_{rj}W_{s’j’}$ appeared, where weight terms isolating all places this weight term appears, the term vanishes in expectation except for terms that match indices of weights. This is in fact true in the asymptotic sense, because the influence of elements of weights on elements of $z$ will diminish with an $O(1/d)$ rate. This step allowed me to then enforce the equality of indices $r=s$ and proceed the analysis from there. The fatal issue with this analysis is that it discounts the fact that while the term does decay with $O(1/d)$ rate, the number of $r\neq s$ terms is a factor $O(d^2)$ larger than the $O(r=s)$ terms because they have one more free summation over an index with $d$ terms. Therefore, for the $r=s$ case we have $O(d)$ terms of order $O(1)$, amounting to $O(d)$ total contribution, and in the $r\neq s$ case we have $O(d^2)$ terms of order $O(1/d)$, amounting to a similar $O(d)$ total contribution.

Our Refined Strategy

Proceeding similar to before, we want to evaluate the first moment. But here, our overall strategy will be very different to compute expectations and error terms: we will now pack every term that is directly dependent on $W^l$, meaning the weight terms themselves and the pre-activations $z^{l+1}$. The reasoning is as follows: conditioned on knowing the norms and angles of $\phi(z^{l-1}(x)),\phi(z^{l-1}(x’))$, it is sufficient to compute the expectation of these aforementioned terms. The highly important nuance is that, these norms and angles have a high degree of concentration. Because, due to CLT, the deviation of the average inner product from two vectors with $n$ i.i.d. elements, will be highly concentrated around its expected value, and its variance will decay as $1/\sqrt{n}$. However, under finite third moment assumptions about the activations, the CLT gives us light-tailed bounds, meaning that these deviations will be within $O(1/\sqrt{n})$ of their expected values with a high probability, where the constant on the deviation $c$ appears exponentially in our tail bound $\text{failure probability}\approx \exp( - \alpha c)$. Therefore, we can use union bounds over all layers to guarantee this type of concentration across all layers. Assuming for now that depth is only a constant and not growing with width, we can assume these $O(1/\sqrt{\text{width}})$ approximation factors hold for all “sample mean vs. expectation” steps in our analysis. After plugging these approximation factors, namely using Taylor expansions around the expected values, we will obtain $1+O(1/\sqrt{n})$ corrections over the final result, which are multiplicative error factors that will converge to $1$ as width increases. That said, these error factors could become significant and complicate a later second-order analysis. But as we learn in this section, even the first order seems to be more complicated than previously thought and we leave the second order correction for a separate analysis.

Let us define a quantity that will be useful throughout our correct NTK results: \(\begin{align} C^l_{f,g} &:=\mathbb{E}[f(z)\,g(z')] \quad \text{where } (z,z')\sim \mathcal{N}\left(0, \Sigma^{l-1}\right)\\ Q_f^{l} &:= \mathbb{E}[f(z)^2] \quad \text{where } z \sim \mathcal{N}\left(0, \Sigma^{l-1}_{1,1}\right) \end{align}\)

We already had introduced the notation $\dot\Sigma^k(x,x’):=\mathbb{E} [\phi’(z)\phi’(z’)]$ where $(z,z’)\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma^{k-1}(x,x’))$, which is a special case of our new operator. The reason for the choice of indexing with $C^l$ being based on $\Sigma^{l-1}$ is that now, we can simplify expressions such as $\mathbb{E} [f(z_i^k(x)) g(z^k_j(x’))]$ as $C^k_{f,g}$. In other words, the correct indexing will be the one that matches the superscript of $C$ with the index of $z$, which is more intuitive than if there was some offset. This definition is also more appealing as it makes a very explicit reference to the function which we are taking expectation. With this definition we have:

\[M_{k,l} =\frac{C^k_{\phi',\phi'}}{d_l} \sum_{i=1}^{d_l} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{d_k} \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial h^k_j} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial h^k_j}\right]\]

Now, similar to before, we will unroll the chain rule formula from $k$ onto $k+1$ but this time with respect to post-activations, i.e., from $h^k$ to $h^{k+1}$:

\[\begin{align} M_{k,l}&= \frac{C^k_{\phi',\phi'}}{d_l} \sum_{i,j,s,r} \mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial h^{k+1}_s}\frac{\partial h^{k+1}_s(x)}{\partial h^k_j} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial h^{k+1}_r}\frac{\partial h^{k+1}_r(x')}{\partial h^k_j}\right] \\ &=\frac{C^k_{\phi',\phi'}}{d_l} \sum_{i,j,s,r} \mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial h^{k+1}_s}\phi'(z^{k+1}_s(x)) W^k_{sj} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial h^{k+1}_r}\phi'(z^{k+1}_r(x')) W^k_{rj} \right] \\ &=\frac{C^k_{\phi',\phi'}}{d_l} \sum_{i,s,r} \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial h^{k+1}_s} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial h^{k+1}_r}\right]\cdot \underbrace{\sum_{j} \mathbb{E} \left[\phi'(z^{k+1}_s(x))\phi'(z^{k+1}_r(x')) W^k_{sj} W^k_{rj} \right] }_{T_{rs}:=} \end{align}\]

Note that $z^{k+1} = W^k h^k + b^k$. Thus, in the last step, we invoked our packing argument of all terms directly involving $W^k$, assuming variance and covariances of the previous layer are equal to their mean-field values.

\[T_{rs}= \sum_{j}\mathbb{E} \left[\phi'\left( \sum_{j=1}^{d_k} W_{sj}^k h_j^k(x) + b_s^k\right)\phi'\left( \sum_{j=1}^{d_k} W_{rj}^k h_j^k(x') + b_r^k\right) W^k_{sj} W^k_{rj} \right]\]

Here we can prove a very useful Lemma based on Stein’s lemma:

Lemma (Extended Stein’s Lemma). Let $(X,Y,Z)$ be a zero-mean jointly Gaussian vector with variances \(\text{Var}(X)=\sigma_X^2,\quad \text{Var}(Y)=\sigma_Y^2,\quad \text{Var}(Z)=\sigma_Z^2,\) and covariances \(\text{Cov}(X,Y)=\sigma_{XY},\quad \text{Cov}(X,Z)=\sigma_{XZ},\quad \text{Cov}(Y,Z)=\sigma_{YZ}.\) Then for any twice-differentiable $f$ with the necessary integrability, \(\begin{align} \mathbb{E}[f(X)\,Y] &=\sigma_{XY}\,\mathbb{E}[f'(X)] \\ \mathbb{E}[f(X)\,Y^2] &=\sigma_Y^2\,\mathbb{E}[f(X)] \;+\;\sigma_{XY}^2\,\mathbb{E}[f''(X)] \\ \mathbb{E}[f(X)\,f(Y)\,Z] &=\sigma_{XZ}\,\mathbb{E}[f'(X)\,f(Y)] \;+\;\sigma_{YZ}\,\mathbb{E}[f(X)\,f'(Y)] \\ \mathbb{E}[f(X)\,f(Y)\,Z^2] &=\sigma_Z^2\,\mathbb{E}[f(X)\,f(Y)] \;+\;\sigma_{XZ}^2\,\mathbb{E}[f''(X)\,f(Y)] \\ &\qquad +\;2\,\sigma_{XZ}\,\sigma_{YZ}\,\mathbb{E}[f'(X)\,f'(Y)] \;+\;\sigma_{YZ}^2\,\mathbb{E}[f(X)\,f''(Y)] \end{align}\)

It is clear that depending on $r=s$ or not, the result will be different.

Case $r=s$: This is similar to the $f(X)f(Y)Z^2$ case. Inspecting the identity there, we can notice that the only term that is of $O(1/d_k)$ is the first one, while others have a covariance squared term, which scales as $O(1/d_k^2)$. Thus we can simplify these terms simply as: \(\begin{align} \mathbb{E} [T_{rr}] &= \sum_{j=1}^{d_k} \mathbb{E} [(W_{rj}^k)^2]\mathbb{E} [\phi'(z)\phi'(z')] \quad \text{where } (z,z')\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma^{k+1})\\ &= C_{\phi',\phi'}^{k+1} \end{align}\) where we canceled out a factor of $d_k$ with the summation.

Case $r \neq s$: Here we have two independent expectations falling onto the $\mathbb{E} [f(X) Y]$ case. We have: \(\begin{align} \mathbb{E} [T_{rs}] &= \sum_{j=1}^{d_k}\mathbb{E} \left[\phi'\left( \sum_{j=1}^{d_k} W_{sj}^k h_j^k(x) + b_s^k\right) W^k_{sj} \right] \cdot \mathbb{E}\left[\phi'\left( \sum_{j=1}^{d_k} W_{rj}^k h_j^k(x') + b_r^k\right) W^k_{rj} \right] \\ &=\sum_{j=1}^{d_k} \frac{h_j^k(x)}{d_k}\mathbb{E} [\phi''(z)]\cdot \frac{h_j^k(x')}{d_k}\mathbb{E}[\phi''(z')] \quad \text{where } (z,z')\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma^{k+1}) \\ &= \frac{1}{d_k}(\mu_{\phi''}^{k+1})^2 \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{d_k} h^k_j(x)h^k_j(x')}{d_k} \quad \text{where } \mu_f^l:= \mathbb{E} [f(z)], \; z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma^{l-1}) \\ &=\frac{1}{d_k} \Sigma^{k} (x,x')(\mu^{k+1}_{\phi''})^2 \end{align}\)

Putting this back in our first moment, taking into account only the leading order term for $r=s$ case:

\[\begin{align} M_{k,l}&=\frac{C^k_{\phi',\phi'}}{d_l} \sum_{i, j} \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial h^k_j} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial h^k_j}\right]\\ &=\frac{C^k_{\phi',\phi'}}{d_l} \sum_{i,s,r} \mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial h^{k+1}_s} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial h^{k+1}_r}\right]\cdot \mathbb{E}\; [T_{rs}] \\ &=\frac{C^k_{\phi',\phi'}}{d_l} \underbrace{\sum_{i,r}\mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial h^{k+1}_r} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial h^{k+1}_r}\right] }_{D_{k+1,l}}C^{k+1}_{\phi',\phi'} \\ &\quad + \frac{C^k_{\phi',\phi'}}{d_l} \underbrace{\sum_{i,r\neq s} \mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{\partial z^l_i(x)}{\partial h^{k+1}_s} \frac{\partial z^L(x')}{\partial h^{k+1}_r}\right]}_{S_{k+1,l}}\frac{1}{d_k}\Sigma^{k} (x,x')(\mu^{k+1}_{\phi''})^2 \end{align}\]

From the identity for $M_{k,l}$ above we can write and conclude the following: \(\begin{align} M_{k,l} = \frac{C^k_{\phi',\phi'}}{d_l} D_{k,l} &= \frac{C^k_{\phi',\phi'}}{d_l} C^{k+1}_{\phi',\phi'} D_{k+1,l} + \frac{C^k_{\phi',\phi'}}{d_l}\frac{\Sigma^{k} (x,x')(\mu^{k+1}_{\phi''})^2}{d_k} S_{k+1,l}\\ \implies D_{k,l} &= C^{k+1}_{\phi',\phi'} D_{k+1,l} + \frac{\Sigma^{k} (x,x')(\mu^{k+1}_{\phi''})^2}{d_k} S_{k+1,l} \end{align}\)

At this point, it is clear that some other recursion for $S$ is needed. Following similar analysis, we can derive:

  1. Recursion for $D$: \(D_{k,l} = C^{k+1}_{\phi',\phi'} D_{k+1,l} + \frac{1}{d_k} C^{k+1}_{\phi,\phi} (\mu^{k+1}_{\phi''})^2 S_{k+1,l}\)

  2. Recursion for $S$: \(S_{k,l} = 2 C^{k+1}_{\phi'',\phi''} (\mu^{k+1}_\phi)^2 D_{k+1,l} + (\mu^{k+1}_\phi)^2 (\mu^{k+1}_{\phi''})^2 S_{k+1,l}\)

For the boundary conditions, we have: \(\begin{align} S_{L-1,L} &= 0 \\ D_{L-1,L} &= 1 \end{align}\)

We can represent this as a \(2 \times 2\) transfer matrix \(\mathbf{T}_k\) where \(v_k = \mathbf{T}_k v_{k+1}\) with \(v_k = (D_{k,L}, S_{k,L})\)$:

\[\mathbf{T}_k = \begin{pmatrix} C^{k+1}_{\phi',\phi'} & \frac{1}{d_k} C^{k+1}_{\phi,\phi} (\mu^{k+1}_{\phi''})^2 \\ 2C^{k+1}_{\phi'',\phi''} (\mu^{k+1}_\phi)^2 & (\mu^{k+1}_\phi)^2 (\mu^{k+1}_{\phi''})^2 \end{pmatrix}\]

However, under the $\mathbf{T}_k$ dynamics, the off-diagonal terms will also have an $O(1/d_k)$ order with respect to width. Thus, we can conclude that in the mean-field limit, the effect of non-diagonal terms will be vanishing at an $O(1/d_k)$ rate. In other words, we could ignore the off-diagonal terms, which gives us back the NTK original result.

Implication: For the large part, to the extent that we wanted to check if the classical NTK recursion is valid, our much longer and complicated analysis only reproduced that result as opposed to violating it. But the interesting and yet unresolved issue is that, apart from random guessing, it was very hard to tell that this term will vanish in comparison, without conducting the detailed and laborious algebraic work. Perhaps, there are deeper and more transcendent insights that could have informed us about the extra term scaling without having to actually do it. Another interesting result of the above inquiry is that it shows these extra terms, while being small, may play a bigger role if we somehow amplify these $O/\text{width}$ terms, namely in the feature learning regime. In that regard, our analysis shows that their first-order contribution entirely vanishes if $\mathbb{E} [\phi(z)] = 0$ for an activation; these non-diagonal terms can always be ignored. This is because the mean activations $\mu^{k+1}_\phi$ appear in the off-diagonal correction terms. This is quite remarkable, in that, these terms in the first order will be zero exactly (not asymptotically), which might be relevant to feature and deeper inquiries.

Concluding Remarks

The key takeaway from our analysis is that there is a drastic difference between the middle layers and the last layer, in that the last layer is the only one that exhibits first moment kernel shift. Furthermore, we saw that this was a result of asymmetries in the kernel evolution dynamics. This progression from detailed first-principles analysis to the celebrated NTK recursion represents a fundamental advance in our theoretical understanding of deep neural networks in the infinite-width limit.
entry.summary: A first principles derivation of the classic NTK result (no magic), with an analysis that already suggests the scaling for feature learning

entry.title: On the global stability of activation variance

link.title: On the global stability of activation variance

entry.content:
The Dynamics of Signal Norms in Deep Networks

In the study of infinitely wide neural networks, mean-field theory provides a powerful framework for analyzing signal propagation. Consider a standard Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) where weights and biases are initialized as $w_{ij} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_w^2/n_{in})$ and $b_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_b^2)$. In the infinite-width limit, the Central Limit Theorem dictates that the pre-activations at each layer become Gaussian. This allows us to track the evolution of the signal’s squared norm (variance) deterministically.

The variance at layer $l+1$, denoted $q_{l+1}$, is a function of the variance at the previous layer, $q_l$, given by the map: \(q_{l+1} = F(q_l) \equiv \sigma_w^2 E_{z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)}[f(\sqrt{q_l}z)^2] + \sigma_b^2\) This equation describes how the expected signal variance evolves as it propagates through the network. A central question in understanding these dynamics is the existence and nature of fixed points—variances $q^\star$ for which the signal strength remains constant, i.e., $F(q^\star) = q^\star$.

A fixed point $q^\star$ is locally attracting if $|F^\prime(q^\star)| < 1$ and repulsive otherwise. This stability condition dictates the long-term behavior of the network’s signal norms, leading to two distinct possibilities:

  1. Category 1: Single Globally Attracting Fixed Point. The network possesses one attracting fixed point $q^\star$ (and possibly other repulsive ones). For almost any input norm, the layer-wise variance $q_l$ will converge to $q^\star$. In this regime, the network effectively “forgets” the initial scale of its input.
  2. Category 2: Multiple Attracting Fixed Points. The network has several locally attracting fixed points, each with its own basin of attraction. The final converged norm depends on the initial input norm $q_0$. In this scenario, the network can “remember” information about the input’s scale in its deeper layers.

A numerical verification reveals that virtually all commonly used activation functions—such as ReLU, Tanh, and GeLU—belong to Category 1. They exhibit a single, globally attracting fixed point. While adjusting $\sigma_w^2$ and $\sigma_b^2$ applies an affine transformation to the $F(q)$ map, a visual inspection confirms that no such transformation can induce multiple stable fixed points for these standard functions.

Interactive Figure 1: Dynamics of Standard Activations
For standard activations, the map F(q) intersects the identity line at a single attracting fixed point, confirming they belong to Category 1. Use the controls to explore different parameter values.
1.0
0.0

This observation motivates our main inquiry: is the single fixed-point behavior a fundamental property, or is it merely a feature of the specific activations we choose to use? More formally:

Is it possible to construct an activation function with an arbitrary number of attracting fixed points?

As we will now show constructively, the answer is yes.

A Construction for N Stable Fixed Points

Our goal is to design an activation function $f(x)$ that yields $N$ distinct, positive, and stable solutions to $F(q) = q$. For simplicity, we develop the construction for the case where $\sigma_w^2=1$ and $\sigma_b^2=0$.

Intuition

The core intuition is to combine several simple functions, each responsible for creating one fixed point. To prevent these functions from interfering with one another, we design them to operate on disjoint and exponentially spaced input scales. We use a set of rectangular “bumps.” When the input norm $q$ is close to the region targeted by the $k$-th bump, the contributions from all other bumps ($k-1, k+1, \ldots$) are negligible, effectively isolating the dynamics for each fixed point.

Formal Construction

Let the activation function be a sum of $N$ disjoint rectangular pulses: $f(x) = \sum_{k=1}^N f_k(x)$, where \begin{align} f_k(x) = \begin{cases} c_k & \text{if } x \in S_k \cr 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \end{align} Since the supports $S_k$ are disjoint, we have $f(x)^2 = \sum_{k=1}^N f_k(x)^2$. This orthogonality is key. The fixed-point equation $q = E[f(\sqrt{q}z)^2]$ becomes: \begin{align} q = \sum_{k=1}^N E[f_k(\sqrt{q}z)^2] = \sum_{k=1}^N c_k^2 \cdot P(\sqrt{q}z \in S_k) \end{align} We choose our desired fixed points $q^\star_j$ and support intervals $S_k$ to be exponentially spaced, governed by a separation parameter $C > 2$:

  1. Desired Fixed Points: $q^\star_j = C^{2j}$ for $j=1, \ldots, N$.
  2. Support Intervals: $S_k = [\sqrt{q^\star_k}, 2\sqrt{q^\star_k}] = [C^k, 2C^k]$.

This choice ensures $S_j \cap S_k = \emptyset$ for $j \neq k$. To enforce that these $q^\star_j$ are indeed fixed points, the pulse heights $c_k^2$ must satisfy the following system of $N$ linear equations for each $j \in {1, \ldots, N}$: \begin{align} q^\star_j = \sum_{k=1}^N c_k^2 \cdot P(\sqrt{q^\star_j}z \in S_k) \end{align} Let’s define the vector of squared coefficients $\mathbf{c^2} = [c_1^2, \ldots, c_N^2]^T$ and the vector of fixed points $\mathbf{q^\star} = [q^\star_1, \ldots, q^\star_N]^T$. The system can be written in matrix form as $\mathbf{q^\star} = \mathbf{A} \mathbf{c^2}$, where the matrix entries $A_{jk}$ are: \begin{align} A_{jk} = P(\sqrt{q^\star_j}z \in S_k) = P(z \in [C^{k-j}, 2C^{k-j}]) = \Phi(2C^{k-j}) - \Phi(C^{k-j}) \end{align} where $\Phi$ is the CDF of the standard normal distribution.

Proof of Existence

To guarantee a unique, positive solution for $\mathbf{c^2}$ exists, the matrix $\mathbf{A}$ must be invertible. Let’s analyze its entries in the limit of large separation, $C \to \infty$:

  • Diagonal elements ($j=k$): $A_{jj} = \Phi(2) - \Phi(1) \approx 0.1359$.
  • Off-diagonal elements ($j \neq k$): The term $C^{k-j}$ approaches either $\infty$ or $0$.
    • If $k > j$, then $C^{k-j} \to \infty$, and $A_{jk} \to \Phi(\infty) - \Phi(\infty) = 0$.
    • If $k < j$, then $C^{k-j} \to 0$, and $A_{jk} \to \Phi(0) - \Phi(0) = 0$.

Thus, as $C \to \infty$, $\mathbf{A}$ converges to a diagonal matrix with positive entries on the diagonal, rendering it strictly diagonally dominant and therefore invertible. This guarantees the existence of a unique solution for the coefficients $\mathbf{c^2}$ for a sufficiently large $C$. Since $N$ was chosen arbitrarily, we can construct an activation function with any number of fixed points.

Interactive Figure 2: Constructed Activation with Multiple Stable Fixed Points
Explore how the number of fixed points (N) and separation constant (C) affect both the activation function shape and its fixed-point dynamics. The construction uses disjoint rectangular pulses to create multiple stable fixed points.
3
2.5

A Remark on Stability

The fixed points we constructed are not just numerous, but also stable. The function $F(q)$ is analytic (infinitely differentiable) because it is the result of convolution with a Gaussian kernel. For a smooth function intersecting the identity line multiple times, a simple geometric argument implies that if $F^\prime(q) \neq 1$ at the intersections, then attracting ($|F^\prime(q^\star)| < 1$) and repelling ($|F^\prime(q^\star)| > 1$) fixed points must alternate. Our construction, with its step-like $F(q)$, ensures that at each engineered fixed point $q^\star_k$, the derivative $F^\prime(q^\star_k)$ is extremely close to zero, making them all strongly attracting.

Conclusion and Future Directions

We have demonstrated that while common activation functions exhibit a single globally attracting fixed point for signal variance, it is possible to constructively design activation functions with an arbitrary number of stable fixed points. This finding moves the dynamics of signal norms from a “one-size-fits-all” regime to a rich landscape where the network’s behavior can depend on the input’s scale.

This opens several interesting avenues for future research:

  • What are the sufficient conditions on an activation function $f$ that guarantee its corresponding map $F(q)$ has only one globally attracting fixed point? While conditions on $F(q)$ (e.g., convexity) are straightforward, mapping them back to simple properties of $f$ is non-trivial.
  • Can we construct other families of multi-fixed-point activations, for example, with fixed points clustered in a finite interval like $[0, 1]$ instead of being exponentially spaced?

Interestingly, this rich, function-dependent behavior of variance dynamics stands in stark contrast to that of covariance dynamics. In a related work (“Emergence of Globally Attracting Fixed Points in Deep Neural Networks With Nonlinear Activations,” AISTATS 2025), we show that if one considers the evolution of the covariance between two different inputs (assuming unit variance is maintained at each layer), the dynamical map always has a single, globally attracting fixed point. This universality holds for any non-linear activation function. This highlights a fascinating dichotomy: signal variance dynamics are customizable and activation-dependent, whereas signal covariance dynamics are universal and robust.
entry.summary: Can an activation have multiple variance stable points? This post proves it affirmitively.

entry.title: How do you build 1/3 probability with a fair coin?

link.title: How do you build 1/3 probability with a fair coin?

entry.content:
Here is the question:

Suppose you have a fair coin. Given integers $a$ and $b$ where $a< b,$ can you devise a strategy that produces an event with a failure success of $a / b$? You may toss the coin as many times as you like.

I found the question fascinating for a variety of reasons, But before I go on about various hints and my own thought processes. Please feel free to take as much time as you want before reading more on this problem.

My most immediate thought when thinking about the problem was, well, it is easy enough to build an event with $1/2, 1/4, … $ probability by simply tossing the coin several times and returning success if they all returned head, i.e., AND-ing these events. It also seems plausible we can construct events that are the sum of these values. Namely, $1/2 + 1/4= 3/4.$ Happy with my progress, I started to think of the simplest case that doesn’t fall into this pattern, and $1/3$ struck me as a good choice:

Given a fair coin, can you construct an event with $1/3$ probability?

My vague idea is that the eventual solution must be a clever combination of a number of coin tosses that magically return $1/3$ probability. Despite my hopes, I started to note that most of my attempts ended with events that had a $a / 2^k$ probability of success, which is clearly a pattern that does not fit $1/3.$ My next idea (which, at the time, I thought was very clever) was that the magical combination of events must involve the Bayes rule. Suppose I can devise an event conditioned on another event where the ratios of the two probabilities are $1/3.$ All efforts in this direction were also blocked.

At this point, I was given a hint that there are roughly two approaches to solving this, and one of them involves approximating the event. This immediately kicked off an idea in my head: We can approximate any fractional number by an arbitrary precision in the binary base $\sum_{i=1}^\infty 2^{-k_i} $ where $k_1 < k_2 < \dots $ denote the non-zero binary indices.

Thus, if we’re happy with an “approximation” of $a/b, $ we can approximate the fraction as $a/b \approx \sum_{i=1}^m 2^{-k_i}.$ we can design the following scheme: Let $E_i$ be an event with $2^{-k_i}$ probability of success, which we know how to construct. My next thought was that we could construct the main event as $E$ as the union of all events $E_i$’s $E = \bigcup_{i=1}^m E_i. $ My thinking was that $P(E) = \sum_{i=1}^m P(E_k) = \sum_{k=1}^m b_i 2^{-k} \approx a/b. $

I wrote down and implemented this idea in Python as follows.

import random 

# fair coin
def coin():
    return random.randint(0,1) == 0

# success of "k" coin tosses (1/2^k) probability
def coin_power(k):
    return all([coin() for _ in range(k)])

# approx a/b prob, B: bits of precision 
def approx_prob(a, b, B = 10):
    p = a / b 
    p_int = int(p * 2**B)
    p_bits = [int((p_int & (1<<i)) > 0) for i in range(B-1,-1,-1)]
    non_zero_bits = [(i+1) for i,b in enumerate(p_bits) if b > 0]

    return any([coin_power(i) for i in non_zero_bits])

def test_prob(f, num_samples=100000):
    return sum([f() for _ in range(num_samples)])/num_samples

test_prob(lambda: approx_prob(1, 3))

# result = 0.3121 ...

To my surprise, the empirical likelihood of the event $0.3121…$ was slightly off from the expected one of $0.3333…$ no matter how many bits of precision and samples I used: A careful consideration reveals a flaw in my original reasoning for $P(E) = \sum_{i=1}^m P(E_i)$: In order to have probability of event equal to sum of individual events, they need to be disjoint: $P(E_i \wedge E_j ) = 0,\forall i\neq j,$ which is not the case if they are independent.

At this point, a hint suggested that rejection sampling might be a good way to solve this problem. To anyone who is familiar with this concept, this should immediately ring a bell: we can use the coin to define a uniform sampling over any set of power-of-two sizes: for a set of size $2^k$, we can toss $k$ coins and represent them jointly as a binary number $i = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} i_j\cdot 2^k$ where $i \in [0,2^k-1]$ can be used as the index of the element in the set. We can assume WLOG that $2^k \ge b$. The magic of the rejection sample kicks in here: if we simply reject events $i > b,$ in the remaining events, $i$ is a uniform sample over $0, …, b-1$, which is exactly what we want! However, we are left with some rejections. What should we do? Well, sample again! Here’s a python implementation:

import random 

# fair coin
def coin():
    return random.randint(0,1) == 0

# success of "k" coin tosses (1/2^k) probability
def coin_power(k):
    return all([coin() for _ in range(k)])

def rejection_sampling(a, b):
    k = 1
    while 2**k< b:
        k += 1
    i = b + 1
    while i >= b:
        i = sum([int(coin())*2**i for i in range(k)])
    return (i < a) 

def test_prob(f, num_samples=1000000):
    return sum([f() for _ in range(num_samples)])/num_samples

test_prob(lambda: rejection_sampling(1, 3))

This time, the result $0.333084… $ and the sample mean gets arbitrarily clsoe to $1/3$ as we increase the sample size.

Now, at this point, I was still left with one big daunting question: Is this the most sample-efficient way of going about this problem? In other words, how many random bits does this process consume? Let us assume that $a/b$ is already the smallest fraction ($a$ and $b$’s common denominator is $1$). Clearly, if $b$ is a power of $2$, $b = 2^k$, the process ends deterministically in one step and thus consumes $k = \lceil \log_2(b)\rceil $ random bits. Now, let us assume that $b$ is not a power of two, and we pick the $k$ corresponding to the smallest power of $2.$ In othre words, $b \in (2^{k-1},2^{k}).$ Now, considering that the event is not rejected with probability $b / 2^k,$ we can see that for any value of $b,$ we accept with $ b/ 2^k > 2^{k-1} / 2^k = 1/2$ probability. Thus, on average, we use $2 \lceil \log_2(b)\rceil $ random bits for this process. We can also derive a high-probability bound by observing that the event of having more than $T$ rounds is upper bounded by $2^{-T-1} + 2^{-T-2} + \dots = 2^{-T}.$ Thus, we use at most $T \lceil \log_2(b)\rceil $ bits with $1 - 2^{-T}$ probability.

While this all seemed nice and good, I was still feeling a bit uneasy. More specifically, even for a simple event like $1/3,$ we can’t use a finite number of coin tosses to build this probability! In some sense, I was instinctually convinced that there is some clever way of constructing a finite number of coin tosses that lead to a $1/3$ probability. To my surprise (!), this seems to be impossible. So I sat about proving that it is genuinely impossible to use a finite number of random bits to construct an event with $1/3$ probability. As strong and daunting as that sentence might sound, the proof is extremely simple and straightforward.

In fact, any arbitrary and complex strategy that you take with random bits can be effectively mapped to a binary tree, with each node representing a random bit and the left (right) leaf of each node corresponding to an outcome of that bit (or coin toss). Finally, the leaves of this tree are the places where you designate an outcome (which could be True or False). Upon this abstraction, it is very easy to see that if our strategy guarantees a finite number of random bits or coin tosses, this implies a finite depth for this binary tree. Let’s say the depth of the tree is bounded by $k$. Therefore, probability of any leaf is of the form $2^{-l}$ where $0\le l\le k.$ Since any success leaf corresponds to a disjoint event with a negative power of two probability $2^{-k}$, the overall success probability equals the sum of negative powers of two. This has an immediate and very important revelation: the success probability of the root of the tree can be represented as a floating point in binary basis with at most k bits. For example, any event like $1/4, 3/8, 7/16$, and so on satisfies this. However, $1/3$ is clearly not representable on a binary basis with finite bits. This shows that the construction gave before was actually exactly tight in terms of its worst case rand bit complexity. This completes the proof that $1/3$ event cannot be produced if we only have a finite number of bits.

I thought this was a super cool and interesting observation from an almost ridiculously simple-sounding problem. I hope you enjoyed the read!
